items.feature: Subject vs object particles: 친구가 subject, 물을 object

corpusAnchor.note: The same sentence as 'I drink water' with one swap: 친구가 instead of 저는. The particles do the work; the verb never changes for the subject.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite Korean rendering that preserves my friend drinks water and the tested feature. Do not change the actor, polarity, place relation, or register.

items.feature: Destination particle 에 and polite present ending

corpusAnchor.note: The subject stays first — it's the VERB that moves to the end. And 'to' isn't a separate word in front; it's the particle 에 glued onto the back of 가게 (store).

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite Korean rendering that preserves i go to the store and the tested feature. Do not change the actor, polarity, place relation, or register.

items.feature: Action location 에서 vs destination 에; object particle 를

corpusAnchor.note: Four pieces now: subject, then place, then object, then verb. 에서 (not just 에) marks where an action happens — a small preview of Module 2. Typical order is S–Place–O–V, but the particles do the real work.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite Korean rendering that preserves i study korean at school and the tested feature. Do not change the actor, polarity, place relation, or register.

items.feature: Topic particle 는 and polite copula 이에요

corpusAnchor.note: The copula glues onto the noun itself: 선생님 + 이에요. After a consonant it's 이에요; after a vowel, 예요.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite Korean rendering that preserves my mother is a teacher and the tested feature. Do not change the actor, polarity, place relation, or register.

items.feature: Topic particle 는, object particle 를, negation 몰라요
items.expectedReadingEnglish: My little sibling doesn't know Korean.

corpusAnchor.note: Not-knowing is its own verb — 모르다, not 안 알다. 르-irregular: 몰라요, like 배불러요.

items.feature: Documented literal gap: time-[subject] not-exist; omitted possessor / subject

corpusAnchor.note: A structure with no English twin: Korean says 'time not-exists' rather than 'I don't have time.' The owner (me) is simply understood and dropped — Korean omits anything obvious from context.

items.feature: Documented literal gap: 회사 literally “company”; omitted subject; office-at 에서
items.expectedReadingEnglish: I am working at the office now.

corpusAnchor.note: 회사 is literally 'company', but 회사에서 일해요 is just 'I'm at work'. 일하다 = 일 (work) + 하다 (do) → 일해요.

items.feature: Non-obvious additive 도 replaces the object particle; polite ending

corpusAnchor.note: 도 doesn't stack on 을/를 — it replaces it. 음악을도 is wrong; 음악도 carries both 'object' and 'also' at once.

items.feature: Omitted subject, past tense, destination particle 에

corpusAnchor.note: Destinations keep 에 even in the past. 가다 → 갔어요 — the ㅏ stem and 았 merge into one syllable.

items.feature: Topic 은 and locative 에 for living (distinguished from action-place 에서)

corpusAnchor.note: 우리 가족 — 'our family' even when you mean yours alone. And 살다 takes 에, not 에서: where you live is where you exist, not where you act.
